title: The New Producer

jokes.text: That sign says 'applesauce.' No, I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'
jokes.setup: Warm-up guy points to the flashing sign, saying it says 'applesauce'
jokes.punchline: Immediately corrects himself — it says 'applause' — cheap misdirection to loosen up the audience
jokes.explanation: Deliberately hackneyed warm-up comedian material. The joke IS that it's a terrible, tired bit — contextually functional but intentionally low-grade. Scores low on craft because it's supposed to be bad, which is the meta-joke of showing a pre-show warm-up.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That sign says "applesauce." No, I'm kidding. It says "applause."

jokes.text: And now, because he couldn't find the exit door... Larry Sanders!
jokes.setup: Standard late-night announcer intro building up the host
jokes.punchline: Subverts the grand intro by implying Larry only ended up on stage by accident — can't find the exit
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economic subversion of the pompous late-night intro format. The joke quietly deflates Larry's ego right at the top of the show, which is perfectly in keeping with the series' satirical DNA. Good economy and structure; works better in context than out.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: And now, because he couldn't find the exit door... Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Mike Tyson was quoted as saying 'I'm in love with myself.' Sorry, girls. That's it. That's that joke.
jokes.setup: Larry delivers the Tyson 'in love with myself' quote building toward a punchline
jokes.punchline: 'Sorry, girls' — then immediately, flatly acknowledges the joke is over and it wasn't much
jokes.explanation: The real joke is Larry's self-aware meta-commentary — 'That's it. That's that joke' — collapsing the late-night monologue format in real time. It's the show satirizing its own monologue while performing one. Great character integration: only a Larry Sanders type of host would be this nakedly disappointed in his own material on air.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Mike Tyson was quoted as saying "I'm in love with myself." Sorry, girls. That's it. That's that joke.

jokes.text: They're using the young Elvis stamp for standard mail... and the old Elvis stamp for packages over 300 pounds.
jokes.setup: The US Post Office is using both Elvis stamps
jokes.punchline: The fat Elvis stamp is for packages over 300 pounds — implying the stamp matches the weight of the package/person
jokes.explanation: Solid, clean topical monologue joke of the era — the Elvis stamp debate was a real cultural moment in the early '90s. Well-structured, punchy delivery implied, but it's a fairly standard late-night joke that could belong to any host. Functional craft, average impact.

dialogue.line: They're using the young Elvis stamp for standard mail and the old Elvis stamp for packages over 300 pounds.

jokes.text: To Artie, get well soon, who's watching at home. Our producer Artie. Don't flip around, anybody. We'll be right back.
jokes.setup: Larry gives a warm shout-out to his sick producer mid-show
jokes.punchline: Immediately pivots to 'Don't flip around' — the producer shout-out and the ratings concern are equally urgent to Larry
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the juxtaposition — a genuinely warm gesture immediately undercut by naked self-interest. Pure Larry character comedy: he cares about Artie and his ratings in the same breath with equal weight. Understated and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Cesario
dialogue.line: Maybe she just didn't tell him where she put his medication.

jokes.text: I'm amazed by these people who are married 60, 70 years... 'That's love.' Well, maybe it's love. Maybe she just didn't tell him where she put his medication.
jokes.setup: Heartwarming observation about couples married 70 years — husband dies a week after wife, everyone says 'that's love'
jokes.punchline: Maybe she just didn't tell him where she put his medication — implying she deliberately withheld it
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark pivot on a sentimental premise. The structure is excellent — the buildup genuinely leads you to expect a sweet observation before delivering a darkly comic murder implication. Well-earned, not cheap, and the specificity of 'medication' is funnier than any more dramatic alternative. This is the monologue's best joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Arthur, come back soon. We miss your cigar smoke in the hallway.

jokes.text: Yes, Arthur, come back soon. We miss your cigar smoke in the hallway.
jokes.setup: Larry and Hank are giving on-air get-well wishes to Artie
jokes.punchline: Hank's specific complaint — the cigar smoke — framed as something they 'miss,' revealing his actual feelings about Artie
jokes.explanation: Economical character beat — the cigar detail is specific and suggests Hank's passive aggression is barely contained even on-air. Works within the mockery of late-night sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Horseshit. Not once in six years did he ever invite me up on the stage. Horseshit.

jokes.text: Jonathan, you're doing a wonderful job. How long have we known each other now? 1980, the BBC, when you came over... We're out of time.
jokes.setup: Larry invites the new interim producer Jonathan onstage for a warm introduction, begins reminiscing
jokes.punchline: Cuts him off mid-memory with 'We're out of time' — the public affection is immediately abandoned
jokes.explanation: Beautifully in-character: Larry performs warmth publicly then immediately dispenses with it the moment it's inconvenient. The pivot to 'We're out of time' is perfectly timed and captures the show's central thesis about the gap between performed and authentic emotion in showbiz. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: ¿Cómo se dice "horseshit"?

jokes.text: Horseshit. Not once in six years did he ever invite me up on the stage. Horseshit.
jokes.setup: Larry has just introduced the interim producer Jonathan warmly on-stage — never doing the same for Hank in six years
jokes.punchline: Hank's furious, wounded 'Horseshit' repeated like a mantra — his bruised ego exposed
jokes.explanation: Tambor's Hank is perfectly encapsulated in a single word repeated twice. The joke works on every level: it's funny on first viewing as a reaction beat, funnier when you understand how deep Hank's insecurity about his status runs, and 'Horseshit' becomes a running motif that pays off with Artie later. High character integration — this is quintessentially Hank. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: my show is being taken over by a guy who looks and sounds like Vanessa Redgrave

jokes.text: ¿Cómo se dice 'horseshit'?
jokes.setup: Hank has just muttered 'Horseshit' twice backstage; a Spanish-speaking staff member (Nina) hears the word
jokes.punchline: Nina asks in Spanish how to say 'horseshit' — implying she knows the situation warrants the word but needs the translation
jokes.explanation: Incredibly economic — five words that simultaneously callback Hank's outburst, add a bilingual layer, and imply Nina understands the situation perfectly without needing a translation of the word's meaning. The brevity is the craft. Could easily have been a throwaway but lands as a genuinely clever beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What's with Phil's fucking nose?

jokes.text: Qué pasa with Jeff Cesario sitting with the panel... first time he's up there as a stand-up? Jesus! ¡Muy malo! This is a very bad precedent.
jokes.setup: Hank is ranting about the show's changes while inexplicably mixing Spanish into his speech
jokes.punchline: The code-switching into Spanglish in the middle of his outrage is the joke — Hank performing cultural cool he clearly doesn't have while being deeply uncool
jokes.explanation: Hank's Spanglish rant is a solid character gag — it implies he's been drinking or performing some kind of affected coolness with Nina, which makes his genuine fury even funnier. Character-specific but not particularly quotable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.line: She isn't. Let's just leave it at that.

jokes.text: Nina, don't you see my show is being taken over by a guy who looks and sounds like Vanessa Redgrave?
jokes.setup: Hank is complaining to Nina about Jonathan Littman's growing influence
jokes.punchline: Comparing Jonathan to Vanessa Redgrave — a very specific, slightly unhinged insult that reveals more about Hank's reference points than Jonathan
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Vanessa Redgrave — British, theatrical, vaguely androgynous — as the chosen insult is delightfully weird. It tells us more about Hank's insecure worldview than about Jonathan. Very in-character for a man whose reference points are all showbiz adjacent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe you're too easily rocked.

jokes.text: But David Letterman, ¿por favor?
jokes.setup: Hank is ranting about the competitive late-night landscape and the threat Jonathan represents
jokes.punchline: Invoking Letterman — their direct competitor — with a desperate, half-Spanish plea, as if Letterman himself is the final straw
jokes.explanation: Part of the Hank-Spanglish running gag in this scene. Functional but slight — the comedy is primarily in the continuation of the bizarre code-switching rather than anything new being added.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Does this mean we have to start wearing jumpsuits because I think only Hank has one?

jokes.text: Larry, great audience last night. Yeah, it was, Phil. What's with Phil's fucking nose?
jokes.setup: Phil compliments Larry on last night's audience while Larry smiles and responds warmly to his face
jokes.punchline: Larry's internal thought — 'What's with Phil's fucking nose?' — reveals his real preoccupation while performing graciousness
jokes.explanation: This is great Larry Sanders Show writing. The voice-over/aside technique reveals the gap between Larry's performed warmth and his actual, petty inner monologue. The specificity of 'Phil's fucking nose' — not a grand professional worry, just a random physical fixation — is the key. It's so petty and small that it's perfect character comedy. High character integration: this is uniquely Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If there's one thing I'm known for, it's my complete discretion.

jokes.text: Nice to meet you. What happened to Melanie Perish? — Maternity leave. — I didn't know she was pregnant. — She isn't. Let's just leave it at that.
jokes.setup: Larry asks about the previous head of late-night programming
jokes.punchline: 'She isn't [pregnant]. Let's just leave it at that.' — implying something much darker behind the maternity leave excuse
jokes.explanation: Masterfully economic dark comedy. Three exchanges and a devastating ellipsis. 'Let's just leave it at that' does enormous comedic-dramatic work by implying something awful while refusing to say it. The joke is the withholding. Gets a callback payoff later when the actual story (suicide attempt) is revealed — on rewatch this moment becomes even funnier and darker.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.line: She tried to kill herself with an overdose of Halcion. She's okay. Let's just leave it at that, okay?

jokes.text: I loved the thing you did with Damon Wayans and that MTV young comedians thing. May I say, you really rock me. — Maybe you're too easily rocked.
jokes.setup: Network exec Sam effusively praises Jonathan's previous work
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, dry retort — 'Maybe you're too easily rocked' — simultaneously dismissing Jonathan and the exec
jokes.explanation: Perfectly calibrated comeback. Larry is threatened by Jonathan's growing standing, and rather than fight it openly, he deflects with a line that sounds almost reasonable while being deeply catty. 'Maybe you're too easily rocked' is a great line — dismissive, smart, delivered straight. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.line: This business will do that to you.

jokes.text: Does this mean we have to start wearing jumpsuits because I think only Hank has one?
jokes.setup: The network and Jonathan are discussing a major push to pass Arsenio and Leno in the ratings
jokes.punchline: Larry deflects the serious competitive strategy talk with an absurd non-sequitur about jumpsuits — and the aside that Hank already has one
jokes.explanation: Good deflection joke — Larry uses absurdist humor to avoid the real anxiety of the competitive discussion. The Hank detail is character-specific and lands well: of course Hank has a jumpsuit. The joke simultaneously mocks Hank and sidesteps the uncomfortable conversation, pure Larry behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: It was right on Larry's desk, right in a folder under some papers, in a drawer that was locked. Finding the key was a bitch.

jokes.text: If there's one thing I'm known for, it's my complete discretion. — What really happened to Melanie Perish, by the way?
jokes.setup: Sam warns that the memo is not for general distribution; Larry assures him he is known for his discretion
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately asks for the confidential gossip about Melanie Perish — in the same breath
jokes.explanation: Classic ironic reversal with immaculate timing — two consecutive lines that completely contradict each other. Larry says he's the soul of discretion then instantly demands the confidential gossip. The structure is airtight: the boast and the contradiction are not separated by any buffer, which is the key to its perfection. Highly quotable. Strong character integration — this is Larry's hypocrisy laid bare in two lines.

dialogue.line: Unfortunately, Phil's social maladjustment runs so deep that he is unpredictable and volatile. My guess is that he talks badly about Larry behind his back.

jokes.text: You didn't get this from me, but her live-in boyfriend left. She tried to kill herself with an overdose of Halcion. Is that right? She's okay. Let's just leave it at that, okay?
jokes.setup: Sam, who just shared the Melanie Perish story, repeats 'Let's just leave it at that' after revealing a suicide attempt
jokes.punchline: The callback to 'Let's just leave it at that' — used first as a tease for the dark story, now used to close it after the story is revealed — perfectly bookends the dark reveal with the same deflective phrase
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is the absolute inappropriateness of using 'Let's just leave it at that' to close a suicide story — the same phrase used to tease the story is recycled to end it, making Hollywood's emotional evasiveness a structural joke. Dark, sharp, very Larry Sanders Show. The payoff on the earlier callback earns rewatch points.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Larry is just the kind of asshole to read that and believe it.

jokes.text: I got the memo! — How'd you get it, man? — It was right on Larry's desk, right in a folder, under some papers, in a drawer that was locked. Finding the key was a bitch.
jokes.setup: A writer asks how Phil got the memo, implying it was confidential
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity — 'a folder, under some papers, in a drawer that was locked' — each detail more incriminating than the last, delivered without guilt
jokes.explanation: Wonderful escalation joke. The structure builds perfectly: each qualifier makes the theft more elaborate and brazen, yet Phil delivers it completely straight, as if this is entirely normal behavior. 'Finding the key was a bitch' is the perfect kicker — casual, aggrieved, zero remorse. Strong structure and earned laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Now I'm sorry I made copies of this for everybody.

jokes.text: You know, Larry is just the kind of asshole to read that and believe it.
jokes.setup: The memo says Phil 'talks badly about Larry behind his back'
jokes.punchline: Phil confirms the memo's assessment of Larry being gullible/paranoid... while talking badly about Larry behind his back
jokes.explanation: Beautiful ironic loop — the memo predicts Phil will talk badly about Larry behind his back, and Phil's response to that prediction is to talk badly about Larry behind his back, proving the memo right while criticizing it. Tight, economical, great character work. The irony is structural, not cheap.

dialogue.line: Hank is very sensitive about his age. He's only 34.

jokes.text: Now I'm sorry I made copies of this for everybody.
jokes.setup: Phil has distributed the confidential memo to the entire writing staff; they're now parsing its insults
jokes.punchline: Phil expresses mild regret — not for the obvious breach of trust, but seemingly for minor interpersonal friction it's caused
jokes.explanation: Classic deadpan — Phil expresses regret for the one trivial consequence of an enormously inappropriate act. The joke is the complete absence of proportion. Very economic and in-character for the self-serving writers' room dynamic.

dialogue.line: Hank is not 34.

jokes.text: It said, 'As far as Hank is concerned, the show could benefit from a sidekick who skews more towards a younger audience.'
jokes.setup: The writers are reading the memo aloud; Hank has apparently wandered in or is nearby
jokes.punchline: The memo directly attacks Hank's relevance — his biggest insecurity — read aloud in a group
jokes.explanation: The discomfort of having your deepest professional insecurity read aloud by colleagues is the joke. Works primarily as cringe setup for Hank's subsequent overreactions. Character integration is high because this is the precise wound the episode keeps pressing.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: It's not actually here but it should be.

jokes.text: Hank is very sensitive about his age. He's only 34.
jokes.setup: Writer covers for Hank's sensitivity about the 'younger audience' line by offering his age
jokes.punchline: The obvious lie ('He's only 34') delivered completely straight, as a defense
jokes.explanation: Understated and funny — Hank is clearly much older than 34, and offering a flatly false number as if it settles the question is a nice deadpan beat. The immediate follow-up ('Hank is not 34') confirms the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Set designer
dialogue.line: I went through this same shit once with Sajak.

jokes.text: 'Darlene is the most competent person in the office.' — I didn't see that. — It's not actually here... but it should be.
jokes.setup: Darlene reads from the memo what it supposedly says about her
jokes.punchline: The writer notes it's not in the memo — Darlene made it up — 'but it should be'
jokes.explanation: Charming small joke — Darlene inserts herself into the memo discussion by inventing a positive review of herself, which is then gently confirmed as invented but validated anyway. Light but effective character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Very funny. Very fuckin' funny.

jokes.text: What are you doing? — I was gonna move the plant. — Why move it now? — First, Arthur tells me to put more plants on the set. Now I hear from this memo that there's too many plants on the set. Listen, Mr. Sanders... if you don't like the job I do on any particular plant... just tell me to my face. I went through this same shit once with Sajak.
jokes.setup: Larry catches a crew member moving a plant during the memo fallout
jokes.punchline: The plant guy has a whole grievance narrative about the plant politics — and drops a Sajak reference as if he and Pat Sajak had a serious professional falling-out over foliage
jokes.explanation: A minor character gets an unexpectedly rich, absurdist grievance monologue. 'I went through this same shit once with Sajak' is the standout line — the plant guy implies a deep professional history of plant-related trauma with Pat Sajak specifically. The specificity and absurdity are perfect. This is the kind of throwaway joke that makes Larry Sanders Show memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think you can never have enough vegetation. Ask Sting.

jokes.text: I disagree with the things on that memo. — Like what? — 'Like what?' I don't have the memo committed to memory. Does somebody have a copy?
jokes.setup: Larry claims to disagree with the confidential memo he supposedly kept secret
jokes.punchline: When pressed on specifics, he asks his assembled staff if anyone has a copy — revealing everyone already has one
jokes.explanation: Perfect situational comedy. Larry has called a meeting to disavow a memo that he can't actually remember, in a room full of people who all have copies. Asking for a copy in that context is simultaneously mortifying and hilarious. The beat of someone immediately producing the memo seals it. Strong character integration — Larry's combination of paranoia and unpreparedness is the engine.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, my God, we've been canceled.

jokes.text: I can see what's going on. I'll turn around... and somebody put the memo in front of me.
jokes.setup: Larry has asked for a copy of the memo; he then turns around, suspecting someone has placed it in front of him
jokes.punchline: He turns around and the memo is indeed right there — the physical comedy of a man whose paranoid prediction comes true immediately
jokes.explanation: Good physical/reaction beat — Larry announces his suspicion, turns, and is immediately proven right. The 'Very fuckin' funny' that follows confirms the visual gag landed exactly as expected. Earned sight gag in a show that doesn't do many of them.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Is Artie dead? Go ahead. Go ahead. I can take it.

jokes.text: Very funny. Very fuckin' funny.
jokes.setup: The memo has been placed in front of Larry, exactly as he predicted
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, furious reaction — 'Very fuckin' funny' — which is itself funny because his anger confirms he was embarrassed
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat capper to the physical gag. Works fine but is dependent entirely on the preceding moment — not especially quotable or structurally interesting on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's an insult. I'm not acting dumb. I don't know what memo.

jokes.text: This thing about the plants. Let's start there. I don't agree with that. I think you can never have enough vegetation. Ask Sting.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to disavow the memo's points; he chooses the plants as his first example
jokes.punchline: 'Ask Sting' — invoking Sting's environmentalism as celebrity authority on office plant quantity, with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: 'Ask Sting' is a perfectly absurdist appeal to celebrity authority on the least important possible topic. It's also very Hollywood — name-dropping as a rhetorical strategy. The confidence of the delivery is essential. Quotable and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Did Artie die?

jokes.text: Oh, my God, we've been canceled. — No, we are talking about something else.
jokes.setup: Hank arrives late to the meeting and sees everyone gathered looking serious
jokes.punchline: His immediate assumption is cancellation — revealing the depth of his existential fear — shot down flatly by Larry
jokes.explanation: Hank's first instinct — cancellation — is revealing character comedy. The panic is disproportionate to the situation, which is Hank's signature mode. Functional and in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do you believe this shit?

jokes.text: Is Artie dead? Go ahead. Go ahead. I can take it.
jokes.setup: Hank's 'we've been canceled' fear is dismissed; he immediately escalates to the next worst thing
jokes.punchline: Asking if Artie is dead — and steeling himself for the news with performative bravery — reveals Hank catastrophizes in a chain
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'canceled' to 'Artie's dead' in one breath, with Hank's theatrical 'I can take it,' is excellent Tambor character work. Each worry is bigger than the last. 'Is Artie dead?' will be repeated for a third time, building a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What do I need, a fuckin' security camera? I covered that on page three of the memo.

jokes.text: We're discussing the memo, Hank. — What memo? — Don't act dumb. That's an insult. I'm not acting dumb. I don't know what memo.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Hank they're discussing the memo; Hank claims not to know about it
jokes.punchline: Hank's wounded 'That's an insult. I'm not acting dumb' — followed by a genuine defense that he really doesn't know — plays both ways: either he's lying or he actually didn't get a copy, which is its own insult
jokes.explanation: The comedy is ambiguous — is Hank lying or was he genuinely not given a copy of a memo that insulted him? Either reading is funny. Tambor plays the wounded dignity perfectly. 'That's an insult' is a great Hank-ism.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.line: Maybe the fucking coffee will become a little bit hotter. From my own experience, fear is a great motivator.

jokes.text: Did Artie die?
jokes.setup: The meeting has moved on; Hank is still stuck on his worst-case scenario
jokes.punchline: Hank returns to 'Did Artie die?' in a silence — still processing, still catastrophizing
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Hank fixating on Artie's death pays off here — three beats of escalating 'Artie's dead?' panic, the third delivered in a vacuum after the room has moved on. The isolation of the line in silence is the key to its comedy. Perfect economy — three words, timed right.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Think I'm attractive and a great dancer, fine. But let's draw the line there.

jokes.text: Excuse me. Jonathan? Diane here has convinced me that as far as the carpet's concerned, we really ought to go with something more direct. We have a situation here. — I know, Larry.
jokes.setup: In the middle of a serious staff crisis, an interior designer (Diane) has Jonathan's ear about carpet choices
jokes.punchline: Jonathan is being pulled between a genuine staff meltdown and carpet decisions, treating both as equally demanding
jokes.explanation: Good Hollywood-satire beat — the carpet conversation is being elevated to the level of a personnel crisis. Jonathan's calm 'I know, Larry' is the right straight-man response. Slightly underwritten but effective contextually.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: it looks like an old Tarzan movie.

jokes.text: That memo was in my desk in a folder, under some papers, in a drawer that was locked. What do I need, a fuckin' security camera? — I covered that on page three of the memo.
jokes.setup: Larry retraces the escalating security around the memo he can't believe leaked
jokes.punchline: Jonathan reveals the memo itself recommended a security camera on page three — Larry's proposed solution was already anticipated in the document that was stolen
jokes.explanation: This is the best constructed joke in the episode. The callback to the Phil theft escalation, the irony of the memo recommending the security measure that would have prevented its own theft, and the absurdist logic of the situation all converge perfectly. Jonathan's delivery — 'I covered that on page three' — is deadpan perfection. Structure is near-flawless. The joke rewards careful watching.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Horseshit! This isn't about those plants. This is about me. I am those plants, goddamn it.

jokes.text: I don't think I want people to fear me. Respect me, fine. Think I'm attractive and a great dancer, fine. But let's draw the line there.
jokes.setup: Jonathan argues that fear is a great motivator for staff
jokes.punchline: Larry's objection to fear — but his alternative is that people think he's 'attractive and a great dancer' — reveals his actual vanity priorities
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Larry Sanders character comedy. He rejects fear (seems reasonable) but what he actually wants is for people to think he's attractive and a good dancer — the absurd specificity of 'a great dancer' is the killer detail. This is pure Larry: the management philosophy that's actually all about ego. High character integration, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Phone the agent. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death...

jokes.text: Artie cannot find out about this. / Come on. Artie. / Especially the plant thing. That greenery balance on the set has been one of his pet projects for years.
jokes.setup: Larry wants to keep the memo from Artie
jokes.punchline: Larry's specific concern is the plant thing — the greenery balance — framed as a 'pet project for years,' which is both absurd and weirdly plausible
jokes.explanation: The plant obsession is being carefully seeded (no pun intended) as a running joke. Larry's sincerity about 'greenery balance' as a sacred legacy is absurd in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He fired me from that QE2 Fourth of July special.

jokes.text: 'Visually, the guests get lost in all the plants. It's like a jungle out there. Sometimes when I flip past the show on TV... it looks like an old Tarzan movie.' Horseshit!
jokes.setup: The episode has built up the plant controversy; Artie (sick at home) is apparently reading/hearing the memo
jokes.punchline: Artie's roar of 'Horseshit!' at the Tarzan comparison — directly echoing Hank's earlier 'Horseshit' but with more force
jokes.explanation: The 'Horseshit' callback lands beautifully — Artie's version is more explosive and personal than Hank's, and the Tarzan movie comparison is a wonderfully specific, funny image. The word 'Horseshit' is now the episode's throughline, and each usage escalates.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Bullshit. You've gotten an earring to make yourself look younger. What have you done to your nipples?

jokes.text: This isn't about those plants. This is about me. I am those plants, goddamn it.
jokes.setup: Artie is furious about the memo's plant critique
jokes.punchline: 'I am those plants, goddamn it' — Artie's complete identification with the set's greenery as a proxy for his own existence in the show
jokes.explanation: One of the great lines of the episode. 'I am those plants, goddamn it' is absurd, deeply human, and perfectly character-specific to Artie — a man of enormous ego who has poured himself into the production details of a show that may be about to push him out. The line works as comedy and as genuine pathos simultaneously. The economy is perfect — six words that contain a whole character arc. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: And the left ear is the gay ear. When you wear it low like that, it means you're catching, not pitching.

jokes.text: Phone the agent. 'Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death...' Sid Bissell, please. Hank Kingsley calling. 'I will fear no evil, for Thou art my rod and my...' Sid? Jonathan Littman is taking over the Sanders show.
jokes.setup: Hank is so panicked he begins reciting the 23rd Psalm while simultaneously calling his agent
jokes.punchline: The interweaving of desperate prayer with frantic agent-calling — both in the same moment, neither working — is pure Hank existential crisis
jokes.explanation: Hank simultaneously praying and calling his agent is a sublime character moment — it tells us everything about who Hank is (showbiz and religion as equal comfort mechanisms, pursued simultaneously and with equal desperation). The Psalm excerpts punctuated by 'Sid Bissell please' is genuinely funny and uniquely Tambor. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Catching, not pitching.

jokes.text: 'For Thou art my rod...' — 'And my staff. Thou makest me to lay down in green pastures.'
jokes.setup: Hank is mid-Psalm during his panic call; someone prompts 'rod...'
jokes.punchline: 'And my staff' — the word 'staff' in the Psalm gains a double meaning (TV staff/crew) and 'green pastures' connects back to the plant controversy
jokes.explanation: The accidental double meanings in the Psalm ('staff,' 'green pastures') connect to the episode's themes with satisfying density. Whether intentional or ambient, the 'green pastures' echo of the plant controversy is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Call me an ambulance.

jokes.text: The ideas contained in that memo are not my ideas. I do not happen to think we need a younger sidekick. — Thank you. — What is that?
jokes.setup: Larry reassures Hank that the memo's ideas aren't his own; Hank is briefly grateful
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately undercuts the moment by noticing Hank's new earring — proving his reassurance lasted about three seconds
jokes.explanation: The structural whiplash — reassurance to distraction in one breath — is very good. Hank's tearful 'Thank you' followed by Larry's 'What is that?' (about the earring) is a perfect beat: the emotional moment is not allowed to breathe before Larry's attention wanders to something more interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's Demerol, you ass, and tequila. It's a good mix.

jokes.text: What? You mean this? The earring? I've had this for, golly, some time now. — Bullshit. You've gotten an earring to make yourself look younger.
jokes.setup: Larry notices Hank's new earring
jokes.punchline: 'I've had this for, golly, some time now' — Hank's pathetically unconvincing denial, immediately exposed
jokes.explanation: 'Golly, some time now' is a wonderfully specific, unconvincing denial — the 'golly' dates Hank immediately while he's trying to seem contemporary. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If somebody farts in the Xerox room, I've heard about it.

jokes.text: What have you done to your nipples?
jokes.setup: Larry has just called out Hank's new earring as an attempt to look younger
jokes.punchline: Completely out of nowhere, Larry notices Hank has also pierced his nipples — escalating Hank's age-panic makeover
jokes.explanation: One of the biggest laughs in the episode. Five words, maximum impact. The escalation from earring to nipple piercings is perfectly absurd and perfectly in character — Hank's desperation to appear younger has led him to an increasingly extreme makeover. The bluntness of 'What have you done to your nipples?' delivered with Larry's matter-of-fact tone is genuinely funny. Economy is near-perfect: 9.5.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I guarantee you there's nothing in there.

jokes.text: And the left ear is the gay ear. — It is? — When you wear it low like that, it means you're catching, not pitching.
jokes.setup: Larry examines which ear Hank chose for his piercing
jokes.punchline: 'Catching, not pitching' — the elaborate sexual semiology of earring placement, delivered as if it's established fact
jokes.explanation: A period-specific joke about the 'gay ear' lore of the early '90s. 'Catching, not pitching' is the funnier phrasing — more specific, more theatrical. The joke's comedy is in Larry's complete authority on this point and Hank's visible horror.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Drink it, or I'll knock you to the floor, step on your neck and piss in that good ear.

jokes.text: I had a friend who was allergic to base metal. Got a really bad infection. Lost about 90% of his hearing. — Yeah? — That looks very pussy.
jokes.setup: Larry is examining Hank's swollen ear while Hank is already alarmed
jokes.punchline: Larry's friend lost 90% of his hearing — then the immediate: 'That looks very pussy' — clinical horror delivered as casual conversation
jokes.explanation: The escalation of medical horror (90% hearing loss) followed immediately by the clinical 'That looks very pussy' is good dark comedy. Larry delivers potentially devastating medical news with the affect of someone describing a paint color. Very in character.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Never get sick. If there's one cardinal rule in show business, it's 'Never get sick.' It's when you're down, when you show the slightest weakness, that they slip that knife in your back.

jokes.text: I'm sure it's fine. I like it. Keep it. Yeah, 'keep it.' All right. Boy, oh, boy. Don't hide it. Be proud. Catching, not pitching.
jokes.setup: Larry has finished his sadistic examination of Hank's ear infection and sexuality implications
jokes.punchline: Larry's sendoff — 'Be proud. Catching, not pitching' — a callback to the gay ear joke, delivered as encouragement, which is worse than mockery
jokes.explanation: Larry's faux-encouraging 'Be proud. Catching, not pitching' is a good callback kicker — the hollow encouragement is somehow crueler than the initial joke. The Hank-Larry dynamic of Larry being obliviously cruel is well-served here.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I have to admire that little Iago... Jonathan Littman.

jokes.text: Call me an ambulance.
jokes.setup: Larry has just left after cataloguing the various disasters Hank's earring could cause
jokes.punchline: Hank's flat, defeated 'Call me an ambulance' — delivered to an empty room, or to whoever is nearest, with total resignation
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly placed. The deadpan resignation of 'Call me an ambulance' — without any exclamation, without panic — is exactly right for Hank's character in this moment. He's been so thoroughly destabilized that this is now his response. One of the most quotable lines of the episode. Economy: 9.5.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Do you think I skew to an older demographic?

jokes.text: It's Demerol, you ass, and tequila. It's a good mix.
jokes.setup: Larry notices Artie is drinking something; Artie has just had surgery
jokes.punchline: 'It's Demerol and tequila. It's a good mix.' — Artie's completely confident pharmacological endorsement delivered post-surgery
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Artie. The authority with which he endorses Demerol-and-tequila as a post-surgical cocktail — 'It's a good mix' — is perfect Rip Torn. The 'you ass' directed at Larry is also very Artie: affectionate contempt. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You want to sit there while Kathie Lee prattles on in your good ear about how Frank hates to change Cody's poopy diapers?

jokes.text: If somebody farts in the Xerox room, I've heard about it. Listen. Nothing gets by me. Nothing.
jokes.setup: Artie claims to know everything that happens on the show even from his sick bed
jokes.punchline: The specific example chosen — 'if somebody farts in the Xerox room' — as the benchmark of his omniscience
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'the Xerox room' as the locale of maximum intelligence-gathering is a great choice — it's a real place in a real office, specific enough to be funny. Artie's grandiose producer-as-god self-image is perfectly captured. The repetition of 'Nothing gets by me. Nothing' with the pause between is good rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hello, you worthless piece of shit!

jokes.text: What the hell's in your ear? — Earring. — Get rid of it, for God's sake. — I can't. Larry wants me to keep it.
jokes.setup: Artie, who 'nothing gets by,' immediately notices Hank's earring
jokes.punchline: Hank's defeated 'I can't. Larry wants me to keep it.' — he's been so broken by Larry's endorsement that he's now committed to a painful, infected earring as if ordered
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Artie's omniscience claim is immediately borne out by spotting the earring, and Hank's passive 'Larry wants me to keep it' is pathetic in the best way. The earring plotline continues to pay dividends.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: "Cousins Will Fuck" is the first topic.

jokes.text: Never get sick. If there's one cardinal rule in show business, it's 'Never get sick.' It's when you're down, when you show the slightest weakness... that they slip that knife in your back.
jokes.setup: Artie is dispensing showbiz wisdom from his sickbed — having just had surgery
jokes.punchline: Artie delivering the 'Never get sick' wisdom while visibly sick, post-surgery, drunk on Demerol and tequila — the irony is the joke
jokes.explanation: The irony of Artie dispensing 'Never get sick' advice from the most visibly sick position possible is well-earned. The whole speech has the authority of genuine wisdom, which makes the hypocrisy funnier. Very Artie — he always speaks with maximum conviction regardless of his circumstances.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but that knife was wielded by a relative stranger.

jokes.text: Drink it, or I'll knock you to the floor, step on your neck and piss in that good ear.
jokes.setup: Artie is offering Hank a drink; Hank declines because he has a show tonight
jokes.punchline: Artie's escalating threat — a remarkably specific and brutal ultimatum — delivered with the warmth of a man offering a glass of water
jokes.explanation: One of the best Artie lines in the episode. The specificity of the threat ('step on your neck and piss in that good ear') is magnificent — the callback to Hank's infected ear ('that good ear') makes it a perfect double threat. The warmth of delivery implied by Rip Torn's style against the brutality of the content is the engine of the joke. Highly quotable. Near-anchor quality for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: swelling it to such a grotesque size that the skull bursts like a ripe honeydew melon. I saw a case like this in Korea once. It was a horrible, painful way to die. Yeah, the screams still haunt me.

jokes.text: I have to admire that little Iago... Jonathan Littman. He played it brilliantly.
jokes.setup: Artie is processing that Jonathan has maneuvered himself into the producer role
jokes.punchline: Calling Jonathan 'that little Iago' — a Shakespearean villain reference delivered with genuine admiration — Artie appreciates the craft of the betrayal
jokes.explanation: The Iago reference is perfect for Artie — a man who thinks in theatrical terms, who respects excellence even in enemies. The admiration in 'He played it brilliantly' while in the victim's position is tragicomic. Character-specific and smart.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You just want people that fear... suck up to you!

jokes.text: Do you think I skew to an older demographic?
jokes.setup: Hank has worked up the courage to ask Artie something deeply personal
jokes.punchline: After all that buildup ('I've never said anything like this to another human being'), the 'deeply personal' question is about demographics — showbiz insecurity dressed as vulnerability
jokes.explanation: The elaborate setup ('I've never said anything like this to another human being / I'm just gonna say it') for a question about demographic skewing is brilliant misdirection. We expect something genuinely personal and vulnerable; we get a showbiz metric. This is the perfect distillation of Hank — for him, demographic appeal IS the most personal question imaginable. Brilliant structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank just threw up in my wastebasket.

jokes.text: What's gonna happen to me? / Too sad to even think about. / Oh, God.
jokes.setup: Hank asks what will happen to him if Jonathan takes over
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Too sad to even think about' is the worst possible comfort — it confirms the fear while refusing to engage with it
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'Too sad to even think about' is darkly hilarious — it's both emotionally honest and catastrophically unhelpful as reassurance. Hank's 'Oh, God' in response is perfect. This is the Demerol-tequila combo doing its work on Artie's social filter.

dialogue.speaker: Jonathan
dialogue.line: but my enthusiastic and aggressive interest in taking his job and producing this show.

jokes.text: Regis Philbin. Come on, Artie. Regis Philbin. He came back. Is that what you want to do? You want to sit there while Kathie Lee prattles on in your good ear... about how Frank hates to change Cody's poopy diapers?
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to convince Artie not to quit by conjuring the fate that awaits him in lower-prestige TV
jokes.punchline: Kathie Lee Gifford's specific oversharing about Frank not changing Cody's 'poopy diapers' — a real, era-specific detail about Kathie Lee's on-air habits — deployed as a horror scenario, with the earring callback ('your good ear')
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly specific horror scenario. Kathie Lee's Frank-and-Cody stories were a genuine audience annoyance in the early '90s, and the specificity of 'poopy diapers' as the nadir of professional destiny is perfectly chosen. The 'in your good ear' callback to Hank's infected ear (Hank is in the room) adds an extra layer. Artie's response — 'Fuck me' — is all the punchline needed.

dialogue.speaker: Sam
dialogue.line: Okay, we're lying.

jokes.text: Fuck me.
jokes.setup: Larry has just conjured the vision of Artie working with Kathie Lee Gifford
jokes.punchline: Artie's devastated 'Fuck me' — two words that contain total surrender to the horror of the image
jokes.explanation: Two words doing maximum work. 'Fuck me' as Artie's response to the Kathie Lee scenario is perfect — not outrage, not denial, just devastated acceptance of how bad the alternative is. Economy: 10. The timing and Torn's delivery make this a standout reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Have I ever told you, Jon, I can't stand the way you talk?

jokes.text: Hello, you worthless piece of shit! Don't worry about us. We have options. Does the name Sally Jessy Raphael mean anything to you? — 'Sally Jessy Raphael'? — Yeah, 'Cousins Will Fuck' is the first topic.
jokes.setup: Artie rallies from his despair to assert he has options; he drops Sally Jessy Raphael as evidence
jokes.punchline: 'Cousins Will Fuck' is the first topic — the specific fake talk show topic conjured to characterize the level of the Sally Jessy show
jokes.explanation: 'Cousins Will Fuck' is a stone-cold great throwaway joke. The fake daytime talk show topic perfectly captures the tabloid TV era's sensationalism in three words. It's both a specific industry joke and broadly funny. Artie's pivot from despair to defiant threat ('Hello, you worthless piece of shit!') to this punchline is excellent character arc in a few lines. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Obviously you guys don't know about my Chinese weatherman. It's "fleezing"!

jokes.text: Yeah, but that knife was wielded by a relative stranger.
jokes.setup: Larry notes Artie shouldn't be up — he just had surgery
jokes.punchline: Artie's retort distinguishes his surgical knife from the figurative knife of betrayal — 'a relative stranger' implies the betrayal by Jonathan (a trusted insider) is worse
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. The wordplay on 'knife' (surgical vs. metaphorical) is perfectly constructed, and 'a relative stranger' does double duty — the surgeon is a stranger, implying the betrayal-knife from someone he knew is more painful. Clean, devastating, quintessentially Artie. Economy is very high. One of the best-written lines of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Remember you held my head?

jokes.text: Please, please let me take this earring out. — I can't hardly see... and the infection is going right to my optic nerve.
jokes.setup: The earring has been infected since the examination scene; Hank's condition is getting worse
jokes.punchline: 'I can't hardly see... and the infection is going right to my optic nerve' — Hank's medical self-diagnosis has escalated to optic nerve territory
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the earring catastrophe. The optic nerve is the right next level of Hank's medical panic — it's absurd but internally consistent with how infections actually (rarely) progress, which makes it funnier. Hank's hypochondria serves his existential fear of obsolescence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We're facing east, so it's actually the sun rising.

jokes.text: Larry fuckin' cares about your fuckin' eye! He wouldn't fuckin' care... if that infection ran straight into your brain... swelling it to such a grotesque size that the skull bursts like a ripe honeydew melon. I saw a case like this in Korea once. It was a horrible, painful way to die.
jokes.setup: Hank is worried about his optic nerve; Artie is drunk on Demerol and tequila
jokes.punchline: Artie's escalating skull-burst-honeydew-melon speech — the graphic specificity of 'ripe honeydew melon,' the Korea anecdote, 'horrible, painful way to die' — delivered as if comforting Hank
jokes.explanation: The standout comedic moment of the episode. Artie's skull-burst speech is a masterpiece of character comedy and dark escalation. The steps are perfect: the dismissive 'Larry fuckin' cares' → the revelation he doesn't → the graphic medical horror → 'ripe honeydew melon' (the perfect fruit; why honeydew?!) → the Korea anecdote delivered as if a comforting precedent → 'horrible, painful way to die.' Each step is funnier than the last. This is what Rip Torn was born to do. It approaches the calibration anchor ('Snip, snap!') in construction and delivery. Highest scores in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I do it because... I love you, you bastard.

jokes.text: Yeah, the screams still haunt me. — So where's your friend now? — Yeah!
jokes.setup: Artie has just described the Korean skull-burst case
jokes.punchline: 'The screams still haunt me' — and when asked 'where's your friend now,' the implication is he died, confirmed by Artie's 'Yeah!'
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper to the skull speech. 'The screams still haunt me' plays as sincere trauma; 'So where's your friend now?' asks the natural follow-up; Artie's 'Yeah!' (implying: dead, obviously) is the darkest possible one-word punchline. The cheerful confirmation of the friend's death is genuinely funny dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm always telling you how funny you are... and how well your clothes fit... and how your ass doesn't look fat in pants.

jokes.text: Yeah, the Whiz Kid! I put up with such shit from this memo. — Get off it! You couldn't wait to get that butthole buddy of yours in here because you don't want anybody in here who will challenge you!
jokes.setup: The confrontation between Artie and Larry over Jonathan reaches its peak
jokes.punchline: 'Butthole buddy' — Artie's insult for Jonathan, delivered with maximum contempt — is both funny in isolation and revealing of Artie's emotional state
jokes.explanation: 'Butthole buddy' as Artie's preferred insult for Larry's college friend is a perfectly crude, specific choice that says more about Artie's contempt than the actual relationship. The drunk fury in the scene makes this feel earned rather than cheap.

dialogue.line: Man, you guys sure have a lot of fuckin' plants on this set.

jokes.text: You couldn't wait to get that butthole buddy of yours in here because you don't want anybody in here who will challenge you! You don't want anybody... You just want people that fear... suck up to you!
jokes.setup: Artie confronts Larry about bringing Jonathan in as a producer
jokes.punchline: Artie's rage-slippage — 'people that fear... suck up to you' — he starts to say 'fear you' (which he's heard Larry explicitly object to earlier) and self-corrects to 'suck up to you,' which is accidentally even more accurate
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence correction from 'fear' to 'suck up' is a subtle callback that works on rewatch — Artie almost says what Larry literally said he doesn't want, then catches himself, but the 'suck up' version is arguably what Larry actually wants. Also 'butthole buddy' is a funny, specific insult that characterizes Artie's vocabulary.

jokes.text: Hank just threw up in my wastebasket.
jokes.setup: The serious confrontation between Larry and Artie is interrupted by an off-screen event
jokes.punchline: Larry's completely flat delivery — 'Hank just threw up in my wastebasket' — reported as a neutral fact mid-argument, derailing the drama
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic interruption. The gravity of the Larry-Artie confrontation is punctured by Hank vomiting — a completely natural consequence of the Demerol/tequila that's been building all scene. 'Hank just threw up in my wastebasket' delivered without emphasis or alarm, as if reporting the weather, is the ideal register. Economy: 9.5. High rewatch bonus — Hank's collapse has been telegraphed but the timing of this delivery is excellent.

jokes.text: I think Sam's reluctance to placate Arthur is based on his knowledge of my... this is an embarrassing admission... but my enthusiastic and aggressive interest in taking his job and producing this show.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to get Jonathan and Sam to go reassure Artie he's not being replaced
jokes.punchline: Jonathan admits — elaborately, with theatrical self-deprecation — that he does want Artie's job, which is the entire problem
jokes.explanation: The elaborate verbal architecture Jonathan uses to finally admit the obvious — that he wants Artie's job — is very funny. The self-awareness ('this is an embarrassing admission') layered over the nakedly self-serving confession captures the Hollywood-speak the show satirizes. Slightly wordy but the character voice is distinct.

jokes.text: Okay, we're lying.
jokes.setup: Sam has claimed 'Sheldon' — the network president — is behind Jonathan's promotion 100%; Larry asks if he can call Sheldon to verify
jokes.punchline: 'Okay, we're lying.' — Sam drops the bluff instantly with zero face-saving
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximal impact. The instant, cheerful capitulation — 'Okay, we're lying' — with zero pretense of dignity is a perfect Hollywood satire moment. Network executives who will say literally anything and then admit they were lying is a great joke about the industry. Economy: 9.5. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Hi, Jeannie, honey? I'll be home around 8:00, okay? Just wanted to let you... Love you too. Bye.
jokes.setup: In the middle of a serious network negotiation about the show's future, Sam makes a mundane personal call
jokes.punchline: Sam's completely ordinary phone call to 'Jeannie' interrupts what should be a pivotal professional moment — the network exec is just a person making dinner plans
jokes.explanation: The banality of the phone call contrasted with the gravity of the situation is good deflating comedy. It humanizes Sam in a way that's also absurd — important meeting, casual 'love you too.' Works as a beat, not a standalone joke.

jokes.text: All right. I suppose we did make one slight, little tactical error. We did not have you on board from the very beginning. But I have to say my most egregious mistake was overlooking our friendship in my somewhat lusty pursuit of this job.
jokes.setup: Jonathan is apologizing to Larry for his scheming
jokes.punchline: 'My somewhat lusty pursuit of this job' — the absurdly academic/pompous vocabulary applied to naked ambition, plus 'lusty' being a very odd word choice
jokes.explanation: 'Somewhat lusty pursuit' is a funny phrase — Jonathan's verbal style is inherently comic, the gap between his elaborate diction and the sordid content of his admission. The scene works primarily to set up Larry's response.

jokes.text: Have I ever told you, Jon, I can't stand the way you talk?
jokes.setup: Jonathan has just delivered an elaborate, vocabulary-heavy apology
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, direct response — 'I can't stand the way you talk' — names exactly what the audience has been feeling about Jonathan all episode
jokes.explanation: Perfect Larry line. It names the joke the audience has been in on all episode — Jonathan's pretentious, overly elaborate speech — in the most direct possible way. The 'Have I ever told you' framing suggests this is a long-standing private irritant Larry has never voiced, now released. Economy is excellent, character integration is high, and it lands as both a great insult and genuine self-expression. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

jokes.text: I think we're done here. — I don't think you want to read that. — What is this?
jokes.setup: The meeting has seemingly concluded; Jonathan warns Larry not to read something
jokes.punchline: Larry reads it anyway — another memo — the cycle of confidential memos being read/stolen continues
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the 'beloved characters' joke to follow. The callback to the memo theme is slightly mechanical at this point but necessary to extract the next joke.

jokes.text: One of Sanders's weaknesses is that he doesn't have a stable of beloved characters... a la Carnac, Aunt Blabby, et cetera.
jokes.setup: Larry reads from the new memo; the memo attacks his creative identity — comparing him unfavorably to Carson
jokes.punchline: The Carson comparison (Carnac, Aunt Blabby) hits Larry's deepest professional insecurity: that he's not Carson
jokes.explanation: The Carson comparison is the sharpest possible professional wound for Larry — and for the show itself, which is explicitly about a Carson-era host trying to survive. The 'et cetera' trailing off is good deflating rhythm. Works as setup for the Chinese weatherman joke.

jokes.text: Obviously you guys don't know about my Chinese weatherman. It's 'fleezing'!
jokes.setup: The memo says Larry lacks beloved characters like Carnac; Larry immediately counters with his own character
jokes.punchline: 'It's fleezing!' — Larry's Chinese weatherman character, which appears to be a mispronounced 'freezing' delivered in stereotype, demonstrated with apparent genuine pride
jokes.explanation: Inspired character comedy. Larry's 'beloved character' is a Chinese weatherman whose entire bit is mispronouncing 'freezing' as 'fleezing' — the fact that this is clearly a terrible, hacky bit that Larry is genuinely proud of is the perfect joke. It confirms everything the memo says while Larry thinks it refutes it. The delivery — Larry performing it proudly, presumably with physicality — is the engine. Highly quotable, high character integration.

jokes.text: Lee and I are going to buy that place we always dreamed about in Puerto Vallarta. Sitting on a veranda over the blue Pacific... watching the sunset... counting the pelicans.
jokes.setup: Artie is still threatening to quit; he conjures his retirement fantasy
jokes.punchline: 'Counting the pelicans' — the retirement dream reaches its absurdly specific, anti-climactic zenith: counting pelicans
jokes.explanation: 'Counting the pelicans' is the ideal landing for Artie's retirement speech — it escalates poetically (veranda, blue Pacific, sunset) then lands on an absurdly mundane activity. The bathos is perfect, and 'pelicans' is funnier than any bird could have any right to be. Very Artie — grand self-mythologizing that ends in something slightly ridiculous.

jokes.text: Like the first week... when you couldn't hold down solid food. Remember you held my head? I don't want some new guy holdin' my head.
jokes.setup: Larry is appealing to Artie's loyalty by recalling their history together
jokes.punchline: The bonding memory Larry chooses is Artie holding his head while he vomited — not a triumph but an intimate humiliation used as an emotional appeal
jokes.explanation: 'I don't want some new guy holdin' my head' is a beautiful line — vulnerable, funny, specific. Larry uses the memory of being sick (vomiting) as his primary emotional currency with Artie, which is both sad and hilarious. The callback to Hank vomiting in the wastebasket gives this extra resonance. Very strong character integration.

jokes.text: Remember that day... when we spent the entire morning readjusting these damn plants? — Listen, you are the one that wanted these plants. — But then you got upset... because you said you couldn't see the Hollywood sign or the sunset. — Well, you know... Well, the sunrise. — Sunset. It's a nighttime show. — We're facing east, so it's actually the sun rising. — West.
jokes.setup: In the midst of an emotional scene, Larry and Artie begin bickering about whether they face east or west
jokes.punchline: The argument devolves into sunrise/sunset/compass direction pedantry — each man insisting the other is wrong, ending in Artie's flat 'West'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The emotional reunion scene — Larry appealing to their bond — is completely derailed by a factual dispute about compass direction, and both characters pursue it with complete commitment. The plant callback, the sunrise/sunset confusion, and Artie's final flat 'West' (ending the debate the way he ends all debates: definitively) are perfectly in character. The comedy of the mundane interrupting the emotional is this show's specialty.

jokes.text: You considered that stuck-up little shit, didn't you? — I had every right to consider him. — Damn right you did. I taught you well.
jokes.setup: Artie acknowledges that Larry's flirtation with replacing him was fair game
jokes.punchline: 'Damn right you did. I taught you well.' — Artie takes credit for teaching Larry to be ruthless, which is both a compliment and an admission of his own moral code
jokes.explanation: 'I taught you well' is a great line — Artie's pride in Larry's willingness to consider replacing him is a darkly comic inversion of mentorship. He raised a show business survivor and is proud of it even when he's the one being survived. High character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: I would dump someone I love just because some new good-looking guy comes along? You know, I'm always telling you how funny you are, and how well your clothes fit, and how your ass doesn't look fat in pants. I don't do that because I have to. I do it because... I love you, you bastard.
jokes.setup: Larry is making his most sincere speech of the episode — asking Artie not to quit
jokes.punchline: 'How your ass doesn't look fat in pants' — the list of compliments escalates to absurdly specific flattery, then the 'I love you, you bastard' lands as genuinely moving AND funny
jokes.explanation: The emotional peak of the episode. 'How your ass doesn't look fat in pants' is the killer specific detail — the compliment-list escalates from 'funny' to 'clothes fit well' to this, which is both deeply specific and oddly touching. Then 'I love you, you bastard' lands the scene: it's sincere, it's funny, it's Larry at his most genuine. The 'bastard' qualifier is the perfect note — this is how Larry says I love you. One of the best moments in the episode. Near-anchor quality for character integration and earned-vs-cheap.

jokes.text: Artie, it is just lunch. Come on. We're just having lunch. I swear to God.
jokes.setup: Artie spots Larry with Robert Morton — the Letterman show's executive producer — at the stage
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate, guilty over-explanation — 'It is just lunch' — is exactly what someone having a significant, show-business-adjacent lunch would say
jokes.explanation: Perfect final beat before the episode's last joke. Larry's protestation ('just lunch, I swear to God') is classically guilty — the lesson from the whole episode about his own duplicity has clearly not been learned. The callback to the Larry-Jonathan dynamic (Larry always having another angle) lands as a great character coda.

jokes.text: Man, you guys sure have a lot of fuckin' plants on this set.
jokes.setup: The episode has spent considerable time on the plant controversy (the memo, Artie's 'I am those plants,' the greenery debates)
jokes.punchline: The outside observer — Letterman's producer, meeting them for the first time — immediately notices the plants, validating the memo's criticism with total deadpan innocence
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode button. The plants controversy has been the episode's running comedic thread — the memo, Artie's existential identification with the plants, the compass direction argument. Robert Morton, an outsider from the competing show, walks on set and immediately, casually confirms everything the memo said with total guilelessness. The final line of the episode, with maximum callback density, perfectly economical, gets the biggest laugh. The structure is textbook: build the running gag for 26 minutes, then pay it off in nine words from someone who has no idea. This is what the best sitcom writing does.
